page: Amazon Web Services m8a.8xlarge is a general-purpose cloud instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features 32 dedicated physical cores and 32 vCPUs powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC 9R45 processor running at up to 4.5 GHz with a 1:1 thread-to-core mapping. The CPU subsystem is backed by 48 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of L3 cache, alongside hardware instruction sets including AVX-512 (F, VNNI, BF16), AES, VAES, and SHA-NI.

The compute capacity is paired with 128.0 GB of high-speed 6 GHz DDR5 memory, maintaining a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory allocation of 4.0 GB per core. The instance provides a baseline network bandwidth of 15 Gbps. It features no local storage and does not include bundled GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses, relying entirely on network-attached storage solutions.

Benchmark outcomes demonstrate top-tier execution across single-core tasks and data compression workflows. The instance recorded a single-core Geekbench score of 2816.0 and a stress-ng single-core rating of 3777.48, placing both in the top 10% bracket. Single-threaded gzip compression reached 41.41 GB/sec, while multi-threaded bzip3 decompression achieved 550.64 GB/sec. Across multi-core benchmarks, the AMD EPYC architecture maintained strong performance within the top 25%, producing a Geekbench multi-core score of 28042.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 79557.66. PassMark database operations scored 40843.98, placing in the top 10%, while static web serving throughput hit 87.72 GB/sec.

Resource efficiency is favorable for applications needing predictable dedicated core performance and fast DDR5 memory bandwidth without the premium overhead of specialized GPU or local NVMe storage attachments. In LLM execution, small 135M models reach top-tier throughput (5311.83 prompt tokens/sec and 378.79 generation tokens/sec), though larger 70B parameter models moderate to average tiers due to reliance purely on host CPU compute.

Amazon Web Services m8a.8xlarge is well aligned for mid-sized relational and in-memory databases, Redis caching clusters, multi-threaded software build pipelines, high-traffic web serving tiers, and general-purpose enterprise application backends.
